title: Under Construction
theme: The root struct: building, arranging and tearing down
objectives: I can use the root struct (build) and a prefix to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can explain how constructive and destructive are mirror images of each other.
I can use the suffixes -ive and -al to tell what part of speech a struct word is.
I can write about a building or repair project using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Struct is one of the most productive Latin roots in school reading: it builds words for physical things (infrastructure, reconstruct), for feedback and learning (constructive, instructive), and for ideas (restructure, deconstruct). Students already know construct and structure, so this unit uses that anchor to show how five prefixes (in-, ob-, re-, de-, infra-) and two suffixes (-ive, -al) change meaning and part of speech. The mirror pair constructive/destructive and the re-/de- contrast give students a way to check a meaning against its parts.

words.def: To teach someone how to do something, or to give directions.
words.ex: The coach instructed the new players to keep their eyes on the ball.
words.ex2: A sign on the wall instructs visitors to wash their hands before entering the lab.
words.nonExample: Staring silently at a student is not the same as instructing them.

apps.academic: The teacher instructed the class to underline the claim and circle the evidence.
apps.spoken: My dad instructed me to wait by the door.
apps.writing: Use instruct when someone teaches or gives clear directions; the thing to do follows to.

cloze.s: The pilot ___ the passengers to fasten their seat belts as the plane began to shake.

cloze2.s: Mr. Park will ___ our group on how to use the microscope safely.

misuse.s: The teacher instructed the students by saying nothing and giving no directions at all.
misuse.why: To instruct is to teach or give directions; saying nothing does neither.

visual.alt: A person giving directions beside a clipboard.

words.def: To block a path or stop something from moving or happening.
words.ex: A fallen tree obstructed the road, so the buses had to turn around.
words.ex2: The tall hedge obstructs our view of the ocean.
words.nonExample: An open gate does not obstruct anyone.

apps.academic: A tall building can obstruct the sunlight that reaches a garden.
apps.spoken: Please don't park there; you're obstructing the driveway.
apps.writing: Use obstruct for a physical block or for something that hinders progress.

cloze.s: A stack of boxes will ___ the hallway, so move them before the fire drill.

cloze2.s: The thick fog began to ___ the pilot's view of the runway.

misuse.s: The wide-open door obstructed the students, so nobody could walk through it.
misuse.why: To obstruct is to block; an open door lets people through.

visual.alt: A tree lying across a road behind a barrier.

words.def: To build or put something together again after it has been damaged or lost.
words.ex: Workers reconstructed the old bridge using the same stones.
words.ex2: From a few broken pieces, the museum team reconstructed an ancient clay pot.
words.nonExample: Building a brand-new house on an empty lot is not reconstructing.

apps.academic: Historians reconstruct daily life from fragments such as tools, letters, and foundations.
apps.spoken: They're going to reconstruct the playground after the storm.
apps.writing: Use reconstruct for rebuilding something that existed before, not for making something new.

cloze.s: After the fire, volunteers worked all summer to ___ the burned barn.

cloze2.s: Archaeologists tried to ___ the shape of the vase from only three small pieces.

misuse.s: The crew reconstructed the bridge by leaving the broken pieces on the ground and never touching them.
misuse.why: To reconstruct is to build again; leaving the pieces on the ground rebuilds nothing.

visual.alt: A crane beside a stack of bricks at a building site.

words.frame: After the ___, workers had to reconstruct ___.

words.ex: The destructive winds tore roofs off houses and knocked down power lines.
words.ex2: Chewing furniture is a destructive habit for a young puppy.
words.nonExample: A gentle breeze that rustles the leaves is not destructive.

apps.academic: A destructive storm can change a coastline in a single night.
apps.spoken: That was a destructive thing to say.
apps.writing: Use destructive for harm to things, places, or relationships.

cloze.s: The flood was ___, washing away fences, mailboxes, and part of a stone bridge.

cloze2.s: Careless campers can start a ___ forest fire that burns thousands of trees.

misuse.s: The destructive storm left every house, tree, and fence exactly as it was.
misuse.why: Destructive means causing great damage; leaving everything unchanged means no damage.

visual.alt: A tornado beside a damaged house.

words.def: The basic systems a community needs to work, such as roads, bridges, pipes, and power lines.
words.ex: The city spent millions repairing its infrastructure after the winter storms.
words.ex2: Without strong infrastructure, such as clean water pipes, a town cannot grow.
words.nonExample: A family's couch is not part of a city's infrastructure.

apps.academic: Roads, airports, and power grids are examples of a nation's infrastructure.
apps.spoken: Our town needs better infrastructure for bikes.
apps.writing: Infrastructure names a group of systems, so it is used without a plural.

cloze.s: Roads, bridges, and water pipes are all part of a city's ___.

cloze2.s: The mayor promised to invest in ___ so that every neighborhood would have safe sidewalks and working streetlights.

misuse.s: A painting that hangs in the living room is part of the town's infrastructure.
misuse.why: Infrastructure means the shared systems a community runs on, not private decorations.

visual.alt: A bridge and an electrical plug.

words.def: Relating to the way something is built or put together.
words.ex: Inspectors found a structural crack in the old stone bridge.
words.ex2: The editor suggested a structural change: put the timeline before the argument.
words.nonExample: A new coat of paint is a surface change, not a structural one.

apps.academic: A structural analysis of a poem looks at its stanzas, line breaks, and rhymes.
apps.spoken: The house has structural problems, not just cosmetic ones.
apps.writing: Use structural for how the parts fit together, in buildings or in writing.

cloze.s: Before the building reopened, engineers checked for any ___ damage to the beams and walls.

cloze2.s: Painting the walls is only a surface change; moving the walls would be a ___ change.

misuse.s: A structural problem is a small smudge of paint on the surface that wipes off in a second.
misuse.why: A structural problem affects how the thing is built, not just its surface.

visual.alt: A building frame next to a drawing triangle.

words.frame: A structural problem in a ___ would be ___.

words.def: Helpful and meant to improve something.
words.ex: Ms. Lee gave constructive feedback that showed me how to strengthen my ending.
words.ex2: A constructive conversation helped the two teams agree on shared rules.
words.nonExample: Making fun of a classmate's idea is not constructive.

apps.academic: Peer review works best when comments are constructive and name a next step.
apps.writing: Use constructive for feedback, criticism, or discussion that builds something better.

cloze.s: Instead of just saying the poem was bad, Priya gave ___ comments about which lines needed more detail.

cloze2.s: The principal asked students for ___ ideas on how to make the lunchroom quieter.

misuse.s: His constructive comments were meant to embarrass his partner and tear down the project.
misuse.why: Constructive comments help improve something; tearing it down is destructive.

visual.alt: A speech bubble beside a stack of building blocks.

words.def: To change how something is organized or arranged.
words.ex: The company restructured its teams so that each group had a clear job.
words.ex2: Maya restructured her essay by moving the strongest example to the top.
words.nonExample: Fixing one typo does not restructure a document.

apps.academic: Writers restructure a draft when the order of ideas confuses readers.
apps.spoken: We're going to restructure the schedule so everyone gets a turn.
apps.writing: Use restructure for a big change in the plan or order, not a small edit.

cloze.s: To save money, the school decided to ___ its schedule so that classes started later.

cloze2.s: After the first draft confused readers, the author chose to ___ the story in time order.

misuse.s: The coach restructured the team by keeping every player in the exact same position.
misuse.why: To restructure is to change how something is organized; keeping everything the same changes nothing.

visual.alt: Puzzle pieces with a circular arrow showing them rearranged.

words.def: Giving useful knowledge or teaching you something.
words.ex: The museum tour was instructive: I learned how the old mill used water to grind grain.
words.ex2: Her failed first experiment was instructive because it showed what to change.
words.nonExample: A blank page that says nothing is not instructive.

apps.academic: A failed experiment can be instructive when the results are recorded carefully.
apps.spoken: That movie was instructive and fun.
apps.writing: Use instructive for an experience or text that teaches you something.

cloze.s: Watching the experienced carpenter work was ___; Jon picked up three useful tricks.

cloze2.s: The documentary was so ___ that the whole class took notes on every scene.

misuse.s: The instructive lecture taught us nothing, and everyone left knowing less than before.
misuse.why: Instructive means teaching something useful; teaching nothing is the opposite.

visual.alt: An open book beside a glowing light bulb.

words.def: To take something apart carefully to see how it is built or what it means.
words.ex: Engineers deconstructed the damaged section of the bridge one stone at a time.
words.ex2: In English class, we deconstructed the poem line by line to see how the words created a mood.
words.nonExample: Crushing a toy in your fist does not deconstruct it.
words.rel: taking something apart to understand it

apps.academic: Students deconstruct an advertisement to find which words and images persuade.
apps.spoken: We deconstructed the radio to see how it worked.
apps.writing: Use deconstruct for careful taking apart, in objects or in ideas.

cloze.s: The mechanic had to ___ the old engine piece by piece to find the cause of the leak.

cloze2.s: Our teacher asked us to ___ an advertisement and name each trick it used to persuade us.

misuse.s: He deconstructed the model by gluing every piece together tighter than before.
misuse.why: To deconstruct is to take apart; gluing pieces together does the opposite.

visual.alt: A wrench next to loose puzzle pieces.

passage.title: The Bridge on Maple Street
paras: When a spring storm washed out part of Maple Street, the town of Fairhaven learned how much it depended on its infrastructure: the roads, bridges, pipes, and wires that nobody thinks about until they fail. The flood was destructive. It carried away a fence, two mailboxes, and a corner of the old stone bridge, and a fallen oak obstructed the only road to the fire station.

Engineer Dana Ruiz arrived the next morning with a clipboard and a flashlight. She studied the bridge's supports and found cracks in the stone. "This is a structural problem," she told the mayor. "The bridge is not safe for cars until we fix the frame that holds it up." She wrote a report, and the mayor found it instructive: it explained what had gone wrong and which repairs mattered most.

The town council held a long meeting. Some residents wanted to tear the bridge down and start over. Others said the old stones were part of the town's history. Marcus, a high school student, offered a constructive idea. "Why not deconstruct the damaged section carefully," he asked, "and use the same stones to reconstruct it?" The council voted yes, and Ms. Ruiz agreed to instruct the volunteers on how to number each stone so it could go back in exactly the same place.

The plan cost more than the town had saved, so the council had to restructure its budget. It delayed a new parking lot and moved the money to the bridge. Six weeks later, the bridge reopened. The old stones were back in place, held by a new steel frame, and a plaque on the railing thanked everyone who had helped.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "obstructed" most nearly means
qs.why: A fallen oak lying across the only road would block it.

qs.q: Which detail in paragraph 1 best shows that the flood was destructive?
choices: It carried away a fence, two mailboxes, and part of the bridge.
The road led to the fire station.
qs.why: Destructive means causing great damage, and the list names what the flood carried away.

qs.q: Why did the council have to restructure its budget?
choices: The bridge plan cost more than the town had saved.
The mayor wanted a new parking lot.
Ms. Ruiz asked for a smaller report.
The residents wanted to tear the bridge down.
qs.why: The text says the plan cost more than the town had saved, so money was moved from the parking lot to the bridge.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Marcus's idea was constructive?
choices: He was a high school student.
He spoke after the council meeting had begun.
His plan fixed the bridge and kept the old stones that mattered to the town.
qs.why: A constructive idea improves a situation, and his plan solved the problem while honoring the town's history.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Old bridges should always be torn down.
Engineers make every decision for a town.
A community can repair damage by planning carefully and working together.
qs.why: The town studies the damage, finds a plan, adjusts its budget, and rebuilds with volunteer help.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built on the Latin root struct (build) and see how prefixes and suffixes change meaning and part of speech. They read a narrative about a town rebuilding a bridge, practice breaking words into parts, and write about building and repair using the unit's vocabulary.

notes.va.instruct.v: Instruct means teach or give directions. Contrast with instruction (the noun) and instructor. Show how in- plus struct gives a word about building knowledge in someone; present that as a memory aid, not a historical claim.
notes.va.obstruct.v: Obstruct is to block. Use physical examples first (a fallen tree), then abstract ones (obstruct progress). Do not confuse with obstacle; they are related in meaning but not in the same word family.
notes.va.reconstruct.v: Re- means again, so reconstruct is rebuild. Use broken pottery or a model. Note a second use, to reconstruct events from clues, which students meet in history and mystery stories.
notes.va.destructive.adj: Pair with constructive on a two-column chart. The prefix de- gives down or undo. Students often confuse destructive with destroyed; the adjective describes the cause of damage.
notes.va.infrastructure.n: Infra- means below, so infrastructure is the system underneath daily life. Have students list five items in their town. Note that the word is usually used without a plural.
notes.va.structural.adj: Structural is about how something is built or organized. Contrast with surface and cosmetic. Show use for writing: a structural revision changes the order, not just words.
notes.va.constructive.adj: Constructive means building something better. Model a constructive and a destructive reply to the same piece of writing. Students may think constructive means positive only; it also names a next step.
notes.va.restructure.v: Restructure means to change how something is organized. Connect to the writing process: moving paragraphs is a restructure; fixing a comma is not. Avoid confusion with reconstruct.
notes.va.instructive.adj: Instructive describes something that teaches you. Contrast with instructional (a different word). Ask students to name an experience that was instructive even though it was not fun.
notes.va.deconstruct.v: Deconstruct means to take apart carefully to understand. Use a toy or a paragraph. Note that the word is used in analysis of texts, advertisements, and arguments.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see reconstruct. The root struct means build. Re- means again, and con- adds together. So I can build it again. In the passage, the crew reconstructs the bridge, so the stones are put back together. That fits the parts.'
discuss: How are constructive and destructive different from just positive and negative?
Which struct word do you think you will use most in other classes?
misconceptions: Obstruct and obstacle are the same word.
Restructure and reconstruct mean the same thing.
Constructive criticism has to be positive.
extend: Sort a list of struct words by whether they refer to buildings, ideas, or behavior.
Write a constructive reply to a short paragraph written by a classmate, using at least three unit words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the mirror pairs (constructive/destructive, reconstruct/deconstruct) two days later with a partner game, then revisit the full ten words at one week by asking students to build each from its parts. Connect to alter, dimension, and culminate from earlier units.

frames: To reconstruct a ___, workers first have to deconstruct ___.
wida.oral: Partner A says a struct word. Partner B names the prefix, the root, and the suffix, and says what the whole word means.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: instruir (also used for teaching and giving orders), obstruir, reconstruir, destructivo, infraestructura, estructural, constructivo, reestructurar, instructivo, deconstruir.
Root meaning 'build' for struct and the part meanings (in-, ob-, re-, de-, infra-, con-) are teaching glosses without origin claims; the memory aid for instruct is explicitly not a historical claim.

Sense boundaries: instruct combines 'teach' and 'give directions'; reconstruct is taught as 'build again' only (the events-from-clues use is in the teacher note); restructure vs. reconstruct kept distinct.
